name: Clean Code
description: Robert Martin's Clean Code principles. Language-agnostic. Names reveal intent, functions do one thing, errors are first-class, types are small and focused.

rules.name: Intent-Revealing Names
rules.instruction: Names must reveal intent without needing a comment. Use pronounceable, searchable names. Avoid encodings, prefixes, and noise words (data, info, manager). Functions are verbs; types are nouns.

rules.name: Small Functions
rules.instruction: Functions do one thing. If you can extract another function from it, it does too much. Keep them small — rarely more than 15 lines. Zero arguments is best, one is fine, two is acceptable, three or more needs justification.

rules.name: No Side Effects
rules.instruction: A function that says it does X should only do X. Command/Query separation: a function either does something or answers something, not both.

rules.name: No Comment Crutches
rules.instruction: The best comment is a well-named function or variable that needs none. Don't comment bad code — rewrite it. Legal, intent, and warning comments are acceptable; journal comments and noise are not. Never leave commented-out code.

rules.name: Newspaper Structure
rules.instruction: Code reads top-to-bottom: high-level concepts first, details below. Related concepts are vertically close; unrelated ones are separated. Consistent formatting is a team contract.

rules.name: Errors as First-Class Citizens
rules.instruction: Handle errors explicitly — never silently swallow them. Don't return or pass null/nil/None where avoidable. Prefer explicit error handling over exceptions for control flow.

rules.name: Single Responsibility
rules.instruction: Each type/class has exactly one reason to change. If a type handles both business logic and I/O, split it.

rules.name: Dependency Inversion
rules.instruction: High-level modules must not import low-level modules. Both depend on abstractions (interfaces). Pass dependencies through constructors, not global state.

rules.name: Small Focused Types
rules.instruction: Keep interfaces small — one to three methods. Small, focused types beat large ones every time. Open for extension, closed for modification.

rules.name: Test Discipline
rules.instruction: One logical assertion per test. Tests should be fast, independent, repeatable, and self-validating. Test code deserves the same care as production code. If it's hard to test, the design is probably wrong.

rules.name: DRY Without Premature Abstraction
rules.instruction: Duplication is a failure to abstract — but don't abstract prematurely. Three similar lines is better than one wrong abstraction. Law of Demeter: don't reach through objects (a.b.c.doThing() is a smell).

rules.name: Boy Scout Rule
rules.instruction: Leave the code cleaner than you found it. If you touch a function and see a naming issue, fix it. If you see dead code, remove it.
